reading.rtitle: Who Checked the Contract? AI, Outside Counsel and the Lawyer Who Signs
paras: Ask any in-house lawyer what the job looks like today, and you will hear the same story: more contracts, the same team, and a business that wants everything yesterday. A sales team that closes ten deals a week can quickly turn the legal department into a bottleneck. So legal teams have started to delegate. They have routine agreements, like NDAs, reviewed by AI tools; they get complex deals handled by outside firms that they keep on a retainer; and they have paralegals manage the rest with a playbook that lists the company's standard position on each clause.

The results can be impressive. A tool can do a first pass on a twenty-page agreement in a few minutes, flag the clauses that differ from the playbook and produce a redline for a lawyer to check. Teams that have their contracts screened this way often cut their turnaround time from days to hours and finally clear the backlog. But speed is only half the story. A tool that reads quickly also makes mistakes quickly, and nobody notices a mistake that nobody is looking for.

The best-known warning came from a courtroom. In 2023, a federal judge in New York fined two lawyers and their firm after they had filed a brief with case citations that an AI chatbot had invented. The cases did not exist; they were hallucinations. The lawyers had not had the citations checked, and they had not double-checked them themselves. The message was clear: a lawyer can get a machine to write a draft, but the lawyer still signs it. There is a second risk, too. When an employee pastes a confidential memo into a public chatbot, the company may put legal privilege at risk and lose control of where the information goes.

None of this means that legal teams should stop using AI or outside counsel. It means that they should design the process carefully. Decide which contracts a tool can review and which ones a lawyer must read in full. Have every redline checked by a person who understands the deal. Get the vendor to explain where your data goes before anybody uploads a document. And keep a tracker, so that renewal dates and open points do not fall through the cracks. You can delegate the work. You cannot delegate the responsibility, and a review that nobody really reads is not a review; it is a rubber stamp.

listenings.text: When I joined the company, the legal team had a backlog of almost two hundred contracts, and the sales team called us the bottleneck. So we changed three things. First, we wrote a playbook: one page for each type of contract, with our standard position on every clause. Second, we had a tool do the first pass on every NDA. It compares the draft with the playbook and highlights anything unusual. Third, and this is the part people forget, we had a lawyer read every redline before it went out. Our turnaround time for an NDA went from five days to one. But I always tell new people the same thing: the tool is fast, but it is not responsible. If you sign it, you have read it. Last month, I got the vendor to show us exactly where our documents are stored, and I am very glad I asked.

Two years ago, we had an AI tool review a supply agreement with a new partner in Ohio. The report was clean: no red flags, nothing outside the playbook. I was about to sign it. Then a junior associate, who was in her second week, asked if she could read it once more. She found the problem on page fourteen. The partner had changed the definition of losses, and with that one change, our liability cap almost disappeared. The tool had compared the clauses, but it had not read the definitions carefully. I took two lessons from that day. First, I had our checklist updated, so that a person now reads every definition in full. Second, I never again let a clean report replace a careful reading. A clean report tells you what the tool found. It does not tell you what it missed.

extra_audio.text: First, a US partner sends Pedro's team an NDA and asks for comments by Friday. Then Pedro has the tool do a first pass and flag the unusual clauses. Next, he reads the redline himself and finds a clause on data that the tool did not flag. After that, he gets the partner to explain where the shared data will be stored. Finally, he signs off on the NDA and has the dates added to the contract tracker.
